Building upon these findings, we extend them to apply to other high-dimensional eigenvalue problems where the eigenfunctions exhibit smoothness properties. The intricate network of neurons within the human brain is a complex system that has long been difficult to replicate, yet simulated with accuracy. This study explores the potential of deep learning models, specifically Recurrent Neural Networks, in replicating the behavior of individual Caenorhabditis elegans neurons. With a vast amount of data available, yet a limited amount of space in the human brain, simulated systems must learn to balance information storage and processing demands. Recurrent Neural Networks, capable of modeling time series data, provide an opportunity to address this challenge. This paper examines the feasibility of RNN models, including Basic, LSTM, and GRU variants, in replicating C. Elegans neuron behavior based on C. Elegans CAGE time series data. Our analysis compares the performance of these models, evaluates their accuracy using statistical measures, and considers the implications of our findings for modeling complex biological systems. The source code for this project can be found at a GitHub repository: https://github.com/stevenkruis/C-elegans-RNN. Our results suggest that RNN models, including Basic, LSTM, and GRU types, can accurately predict C. Elegans neuron behavior based on C. Elegans CAGE time series data. This study demonstrates the potential of these models, indicating a promising future for simulating intricate biological systems with C. Elegans neurons. Future research directions are outlined, including the possibility of simulating entire C. Elegans networks with RNN models, and the potential for these models to inform C. Elegans circuit analysis. Our findings also shed light on the limitations of C. Elegans data, suggesting that RNN models may struggle to replicate Caenorhabditis elegans neuron behavior due to limited, low-resolution data sets. The paper establishes global solvability and scattering in the energy space $H^1_a(\mathbb R^3)$ for all initial conditions in the defocusing scenario, whereas for the focusing scenario, it proves scattering for data below a threshold by leveraging a virial/Morawetz method. Additionally, it shows the existence of a unique soliton for this model and uses the energy-rage method to prove that in the defocusing scenario, the solution remains in the energy norm of the soliton plus a bounded region, ultimately leading to the establishment of almost-morphy in the mass-variance space in the focusing scenario. Ultimately, this almost-morphy property, combined with a scattering criterion previously proposed in Benyi et al. (Comm. Pure & Appl. Math., 2018), implies the occurrence of bound states in the defocusing scenario located below the threshold of scattering. Moreover, in the case where $0 < b < 1$ and $a=\frac14$, it is demonstrated that one can actually obtain scattering for any initial data without any restrictions. This result is particularly surprising given the fact that for $a=\frac14$, the corresponding constant in the virial identity becomes zero, rendering standard analysis methods inapplicable. To circumvent this challenge, a novel approach is developed that relies on the connection between the defocusing scenario and the regularized inverse square Schrödinger equation. This approach allows for the establishment of global $L^2$-stability in the difference between the solutions with and without the potential for any initial data. This, in turn, enables the establishment of scattering for any initial data when $0 < b < 1$ and $a=\frac14$. Deep learning models' success in various graph-based learning tasks has been significant, but they often rely on having a graph dataset specifically designed for their task. This limitation can be comparable to the problems that deep learning models faced when adapting to work with out-of-distribution data. We're exploring the potential for graph neural networks to learn general graph capabilities that can then be applied across different tasks, and examining the feasibility of transfer learning in graph space. We've developed a method to assess the degree to which a model's skills can be transferred between tasks, and found that models trained on multiple related tasks can learn more general skills than those trained on multiple unrelated tasks. This is an initial step towards understanding and developing transfer learning in graph neural networks, and our results suggest there's potential for GNNs to learn more general and transferable skills. We've also found that models trained on related tasks can learn skills that are similar to those learned by human cognitive architectures, and this provides further evidence for the potential of transfer learning in graph neural networks. A collaborative filtering system predicts user preferences by identifying patterns that connect users to similar items. To do this, we use a Bayesian double feature allocation model that groups users and items according to their shared characteristics, where each group represents a distinct feature. The 'double' aspect of this approach reflects both the initial clustering and the multiple shared features of the groups. The algorithm creates a recommendation matrix for each feature, where the values represent the amount of preference associated with that feature for a specific user and item. The resulting recommendations accurately predict user behavior on various datasets, such as MovieLens and Amazon books. Additionally, we compare our approach to existing state-of-the-art methods and find that it surpasses them in both accuracy and computation efficiency. The source code for this project can be found at https://github.com/andreaborracino/double-feature-allocation. The results of the project have been published in a paper titled "A Bayesian double feature allocation model for collaborative filtering" published in Information Systems, as well as another one titled "A Bayesian double feature allocation model with shared items in social networks" published in Information Retrieval Systems. equivalent consumption rate problems, describe time-based costs and objective functions
along with time-variant constraints. In the presented scenario, two patients reliant on

maximize the recovery rates of both patients while ensuring the minimum necessary
ventilator sharing capacity. The solution strategy employs direct transcription methods,
specifically the collocation and residual methods, to formulate and solve non-linear
programming problems. In addition to a comprehensive description of methods and
algorithmic options, the study examines the impact of different hyperparameters on
convergence performance. Ultimately, the approach yields viable solutions that save lives
and minimize the required ventilator sharing capacity. The presented work serves as a
practical example of solving dynamic optimization problems using collocation-based
transcription methods. The associated code can be found at https://github.com/daankeijzer/dynamic_optimization_tutorial. A rational map $f$ from the Riemann sphere to itself is bicritical if it has precisely two points where the derivative is zero. We identify the groups that can be formed as groups of deck transformations of iterations of such bicritical maps, providing a comprehensive classification up to isomorphism. The results also extend to maps with isolated fixed points. Furthermore, for bicritical maps where the points with derivative zeros are complex, we determine the possible groups of deck transformations for any given iterate of $f^k$; in cases where both zeros are complex, this group must be finite. In contrast, for bicritical maps with at least one zero with a vanishing real value, we find instances where the group of deck transformations for an iterate of $f^k$ is not only infinite but also inseparable from the function's action. We use these findings to identify planar bicritical maps whose action by deck transformations on their iterates admits exactly two inequivalent conjugacy classes. We also explore connections to recently discovered examples of maps with non-Hausdorff orbit spaces. Ultimately, our work raises a question about identifying all bicritical maps whose action by deck transformations on their iterates is finite. Such maps likely exist, given our analysis of various examples; a positive answer would yield additional examples with non-Hausdorff orbit spaces. We pose a related open question about identifying all rational maps from the Riemann sphere to itself whose action by deck transformations on their iterates is finite. Such maps may be complicated objects, but understanding their properties could yield significant insights into the geometry and dynamics of planar rational maps. This background study explores recent advancements in processing time-varying matrix problems through a framework of predictive computations known as Zeroing Neural Networks (ZNN). Driven by the principles of analog computing, ZNN algorithms solve matrix problems by leveraging derivatives of unknown functionals that drive state variables towards correct solutions. Derivative-based algorithms are inherently nonlinear and analyze the behavior of nonlinear dynamic systems using differential equations. Due to their nonlinearity, these algorithms are challenging to train using backpropagation and demand task-specific hyperparameter tuning, limiting their adaptability across tasks. This study redresses these drawbacks by proposing task-agnostic linear ZNN algorithms applicable to a broad range of problems, including inverse and decomposition tasks, and demonstrating their effectiveness on real-world datasets. Moreover, these algorithms can be trained using backpropagation, and their performance is comparable to state-of-the-art methods in various applications. An analysis of the computational complexity of these algorithms reveals that they have efficient time and space requirements. Finally, the study showcases the potential of ZNN algorithms as a paradigm for analog computing in the context of predictive and deep predictive computations. Although these algorithms are not truly neural, they share underlying principles and can be viewed as precursors to modern neural network-based solutions, highlighting the significance of derivative-based algorithms in the realm of predictive and deep predictive computations. A key area of investigation is to determine the optimal balance between the underlying mathematical structure of these algorithms and the expressive power of neural networks. This study serves as an introduction to the world of predictive and deep predictive computations, and it is hoped that the insights gained will inspire further research into the development of general-purpose, task-agnostic, linear ZNN algorithms. Moreover, the study identifies promising research avenues, including the exploration of alternative nonlinear ZNN algorithms and the investigation of the connection between ZNN algorithmic structures and neural network architecture, leading to the potential derivation of new neural network designs. In traditional deep learning, the objective is often to minimize the overall error rate.  However, this approach falls short in few-shot learning scenarios, where we need to develop representations effective for each individual class.  Building on insights from metric learning techniques, we propose a method to optimize prototypes for each class.  By maximizing the inter-class variance and minimizing the intra-class dispersion, our framework, C3, achieves this goal.  Utilizing a Bayesian approach to model uncertainty, we can identify confident data points and effectively tackle noisy labels.  Empirical evaluations on various benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of our framework over state-of-the-art methods.  Furthermore, our framework exhibits strong generalization capabilities when applied to semantic segmentation tasks. Recent studies have highlighted deep neural networks' susceptibility to adversarial inputs. However, existing countermeasures are largely ineffective, leading many to believe that natural robustness against such threats may be unattainable. To better understand this issue, we conducted an in-depth examination of the relationship between neural network training loss and adversarial examples. Specifically, we focused on Gaussian mixture model (GMM) loss, which is a key factor in determining the robustness of deep neural networks. Notably, our analysis reveals that GMM loss is closely linked to the spectral properties of the Hessian matrix, a finding that holds true across various models and datasets. Moreover, our experiments show that Hessian matrix regularization can significantly reduce GMM loss and significantly improve the robustness of deep neural networks against adversarial threats. Interestingly, our findings suggest that incorporating additional regularization techniques can also minimize GMM loss and enhance the robustness of deep neural networks against such threats. Overall, our research sheds light on the relationship between neural network training loss and adversarial examples, and identifies potential avenues for achieving natural robustness against these threats. Furthermore, a connection between functional Gaussian processes and the original real-valued case of pathwise conditioning, established by Kuchler and Reitz (2019), is established. Finally, a practical application of pathwise conditioning, relevant to random fields, is described along with an illustrative example. Relevant proofs are included in the appendix. Moreover, a critical examination of the relationship between pathwise conditioning and the log-concave Gaussian process (GP) conditioning problem is conducted, with a focus on distinguishing between these two distinct concepts. This distinction reveals that GP conditioning by addition of another GP is an instance of pathwise conditioning, with the added GP playing the role of a delta shift. This shift corresponds to a specific type of gauge group, as first introduced by van der Hof et al (2020). A ground-and-air sensor network of this nature has a wide range of potential applications, which include disaster response situations such as earthquakes, floods, or typhoons, as well as remote locations such as mountainous areas or areas with limited infrastructure availability. To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems with multiple influencing factors, reinforcement learning agents can effectively utilize previously collected historical data.  Standard experience replay enables agents to retain information from prior iterations.  However, the current approach equally values all collected observations, neglecting valuable insights gained from recent interactions.  To mitigate this, variance-reduced experience replay is introduced in this research.  By focusing on reducing the variance of cost function approximations, this method enables recent observations to carry greater weight, leading to accelerated policy optimization.  The proposed approach has been successfully tested across multiple dynamic environments and scenarios, demonstrating improved efficiency and robustness compared to prior methods.  Results indicate that variance reduction based experience replay accelerates non-stationary reinforcement learning tasks by up to 3 times the rate of optimal policy evaluation.  Notably, this method also enhances generalization capabilities by improving policy robustness and outperforming experience replay in scenarios where data is partially observable.  The source code for this research is publicly available on GitHub, under the repository https://github.com/kuangwenhao/VRExperienceReplay.  Future applications of this method are anticipated to be versatile, encompassing various real-world scenarios, such as robotic locomotion and inventory management modeling as Markov decision processes.  Moreover, integrating this approach with established policy optimization techniques reveals considerable potential for future research and development.  Specifically, future directions for study could include combining variance reduction based experience replay with policy gradient methods and assessing its compatibility with commonly employed experience replay techniques. Two new strategies have been proposed to apply supersymmetry in the study of continuous Gaussian path integrals. These methods are aimed at replacing quadratic terms in path integrals. Specifically, the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization formula have been put forward as potential solutions. In this research, the supersymmetry properties of these two techniques have been examined. It was discovered that the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation is inconsistent when applied under supersymmetry, resulting in an additional term that depends on the bosonic Gaussian measure. Conversely, the superbosonization formula consistently respects supersymmetry but yields an opposite sign for the kinetic term of the transformed variable. Furthermore, the application of these methods to the same Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation step reveals equivalent results, implying that the superbosonization formula can be used as a proxy for the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation. Consequently, the application of supersymmetry to the superbosonization formula is feasible, opening up possibilities for the analysis of more complex path integrals. It was demonstrated that the superbosonization formula can be used to study the supersymmetric non-Gaussian path integral associated with a $\phi^4$ interaction. In doing so, the formula was linked to the appearance of the gamma function in the context of path integrals. Ultimately, the connection between the superbosonization formula and the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation highlights the potential for the synergistic use of these methods in the application and development of supersymmetry in the study of path integrals. It was also noted that the superbosonization formula offers an advantage in the context of more complex path integrals, while the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation may be more suitable in the context of the harmonic path integral. It is hoped that this distinction may serve as a starting point for further investigation into the optimal use of these methods. The application of supersymmetry to the study of path integrals has been a topic of interest for many years. The research presented here primarily serves as an introductory exploration of the superbosonization formula, a relatively recent development in the field. The formula was first introduced in 2015 by Zinn-Justin. It is the aim of this research to contribute to the ongoing discussion surrounding supersymmetry in the context of path integrals and to inspire further investigation into the field. The research presented here is largely theoretical and is grounded in the existing body of knowledge on supersymmetry in the context of path integrals.

Building on existing research, we demonstrate that incorporating details from static models can improve the accuracy of short-term forecasts. However, we also observe that incorporating too much detail from static archetypes leads to overfitting in long-term forecasting. This achievement enables the MoDeRNN architecture to surpass state-of-the-art performance in both short-term and long-term forecasting tasks. Moreover, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the motion details that contribute to successful prediction and identify that both rigid body motion and fluid-like behavior are crucial for accurate forecasting. They also shed light on the behavior of red algae during diel movements, which serves as a real-world example of long-term forecasting challenges. Josephine scripts interact with Rust code, implementing zone allocation and region-based storage.

In this research in infinite-dimensional spaces of functions, specifically in Hilbert spaces related to $H^s$, where $s>1/2$, we studied the Navier-Stokes equations in three dimensions and established estimates for the solution's norm, assuming the initial condition is periodic. These estimates depend on the initial condition and grow as $t^{3/2}$. This work also shows that solutions with periodic initial conditions are in spaces like $H^s$ for $s>1/2$ and $t\leq T$. Moreover, we found that the solutions' norms in these spaces are bounded as long as the initial condition does not exceed a certain critical threshold, given by $||u_0||_H$ in these spaces. This critical threshold gives rise to two types of solutions: regular and non-regular. Regular solutions are in the space of bounded functions over a certain period of time, while non-regular solutions are not. Crucially, we found that the non-regular solutions' growth rate is less than any positive number for all practical purposes, given the initial condition does not exceed the critical threshold and the parameters are chosen appropriately. This work also shows that the non-regular solutions can persist indefinitely as the time goes to infinity. This is an example of a simple steady-state solution that arises from periodic initial conditions and could be relevant to studying turbulent behavior. Individuals who are not proficient in sight-reading or have visual impairments face significant challenges accessing printed documents. The over-reliance on visual cues for navigation and information retrieval in daily life can be a major obstacle. The adoption of digital document scanners and readers has simplified document access, however it doesn't address the inherent navigability issue of printed documents preventing users from efficiently finding specific information. In this research, we examined the navigability of printed documents through an extensive survey and subsequent focus groups, focusing on the needs of visually impaired individuals. The findings highlight the severe difficulties this group encounters when trying to locate specific information within printed documents under normal conditions of layout, structure, and formatting. The results also show that visually impaired individuals heavily depend on assistive technologies like scanners and readers, but still rely on alternative strategies like tactile marks and audio cues for navigating documents. The insights gained from this research can contribute to the development of innovative solutions to enhance document navigability, ultimately benefiting a broader audience including the not-yet-technologically-advantaged group. The ultimate goal is to design a system that empowers visually impaired individuals to efficiently access information within printed documents, mirroring the seamless experience of sighted individuals. The proposed solution is a scanning and reading system that integrates document structure, visual cues, and formatting to facilitate efficient navigation. The system is divided into two modules, the structural module that utilizes Xylophone to extract document structure, and the visual module that utilizes Vizier to extract visual cues. The combination of these two modules enables users to efficiently navigate documents composed of articles, books, and forms, ultimately helping visually impaired individuals access their desired information. The system's reliability was tested through a usability study that demonstrated its ability to accurately identify the required information up to 90% of the time, thereby validating the hypothesis of the system's concept. The system's performance was further evaluated by comparing it with existing alternative solutions like audio and tactile documents. The results showed that the system's average response time is 2.5 minutes, 2.8 minutes for Vizier, and 3.5 minutes for the alternative solutions. The study also demonstrated that the system's error rate is 8.7% for the structural module, 9.2% for the visual module, and 40% for the alternative solutions. The system's success was further confirmed through a user study that tested the system's usability and found that 85% of the users were able to locate the required information efficiently. While BERT excels at modeling bidirectional contexts through denoising autoencoding, its reliance on input masking overlooks positional dependencies, leading to inconsistent pretraining-finetune performance. This has motivated the development of XLNet, an enhanced pretraining approach based on autoregressive language modeling. This method enables bidirectional contextual learning by leveraging permutations of factorization order and, due to its autoregressive formulation, naturally incorporates key factors influencing pretraining language modeling. Additionally, XLNet incorporates key ideas from the Transformer architecture, including multi-head self-attention, to improve efficiency under limited computational constraints. Compared to BERT, XLNet demonstrates superior performance on 20 tasks, including but not limited to model routing, question answering, and sentence classification, achieved through achieving state-of-the-art results with only 25% of the parameters of BERT-Large. Notably, XLNet's pretraining objectives are inherently more challenging and effective than those employed in BERT, resulting in faster convergence and more stable training. This has far-reaching implications for natural language processing and suggests significant potential for autoregressive pretraining in this domain. The study of exoplanetary atmospheres through transit spectroscopy faces significant interference from the host star due to its intense emission spectrum. However, this effect can be significantly reduced by high-resolution spectroscopy, making it more suitable for analyzing exoplanetary transmissions. A recent software package, Spectral Analysis of Rockey Exoplanet atmospheres (EXPECTA), was developed specifically for this purpose. EXPECTA incorporates a stellar correction module that can be optimized for both high- and low-resolution spectra. In this study, various stellar activity scenarios were simulated to evaluate the impact on hypothetical transits, and the software's efficiency in detecting the exoplanetary signal was assessed. The results showed that, although low-resolution spectroscopy is more susceptible to stellar activity contamination, a range of techniques can be applied to improve the signal-to-noise ratio and facilitate atmospheric analysis. These methods can potentially yield reliable results, and the choice of technique depends on specific observational parameters, such as resolution, signal strength, and data quality. This probabilistic approach is applied to a multi-level control system in aerospace flight control, providing an adaptable framework for evaluating system resiliency at various levels of complexity.

1. A practical application of STL formulas in defining system resiliency.
2. A flexible metric for evaluating resilience under uncertainty.
3. A practical implementation of the proposed methodology in an aerospace flight control system.

Our research demonstrates the potential of using STL-based specifications as a standardized approach for defining system resiliency and provides a framework for formal verification and analysis. Additionally, our results highlight the benefits of employing formal methods in designing resilient CPS.

These comprise diverse sources of 3D point clouds, varying densities, and significant registration discrepancies. Existing methods have focused on using local features from map and point cloud domains, but have not effectively addressed the registration challenges associated with dense local features and sparse global features. This paper presents a novel registration approach called NDT-Transformer that leverages the normal distribution transform representation to condense and standardise dense local features, and extracts dense region features and sparse global features to learn a cross-feature embedding space. By doing so, it enables the alignment of local features with global features in dense regions to determine the overall registration displacement. These advancements enable the method to outperform existing state-of-the-art approaches by a significant margin on Oxford and TUM datasets. The effectiveness of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) has been demonstrated across a variety of graph and node classification tasks. Nonetheless, these networks are prone to the limitations of deep learning models, where interpretability and reliance on large amounts of data pose significant challenges. Research has indicated that pseudo-labeling techniques can be effective in addressing data scarcity issues, as they allow neural networks to self-train on unlabeled examples. Nevertheless, current pseudo-labeling approaches are often hindered by incorrect labels introduced by low-confidence or misclassified labeled examples, which can hinder the networks' ability to learn from them. To address this limitation, we have developed Informative Pseudo-labeling for GNNs (IP-GNN), an adaptive pseudo-labeling framework that selectively utilizes pseudo-labels derived from highly confident, correctly classified examples. By achieving this selection, IP-GNN is able to exclude potentially misleading examples and prevent the transmission of incorrect gradients during backpropagation. As a result, IP-GNN is able to achieve improved results on multiple semi-supervised node classification tasks when compared to other contemporary pseudo-labeling techniques. This study presents the first fully verified methods for privately learning decision trees in a hierarchical manner, where data is provided in batches. Two algorithms are introduced, each capable of accurately replicating decision trees on large datasets, even as they grow without bounds. The first method relies on private pruning to produce tree structures, while the second utilizes post-processing techniques on top of existing private trees to enhance accuracy. To validate these approaches, we employed a differential privacy framework incorporating probabilistic models of data and queries to determine the effectiveness of our methods, which are implementable at scale using distributed systems and high-performance computing. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that our algorithms provide the highest level of precision among privately trained decision trees. In addition, we provide a formal analysis of the trade-offs between accuracy and privacy for our methods, enabling distribution and optimization in a more efficient manner. Experimental data shows that our algorithms perform significantly better than existing approaches, both in terms of accuracy and computational speed. Notably, our results indicate that high-entropy data can tolerate more aggressive privacy parameters, while low-entropy data requires more stringent conditions to maintain accuracy. This insight highlights the importance of considering data distributions when applying privacy mechanisms, which is particularly significant for decision trees based on categorical attributes. Ultimately, our findings demonstrate that decision trees offer the best possible trade-off between accuracy and privacy, while our algorithms provide a reliable solution for this problem in a distributed system. Our goal in this research is to develop an end-to-end training method for growing plants through autonomous robotic control. We present GROWSPACE, a simulation environment where a robotic grower adjusts a stem's growth parameters to optimize a target function, such as a visual metric, at each node organically connected to the previous one. We identified key challenges in this problem: (1) efficient exploration of parameter settings to find optimal solutions, (2) learning plant models that adapt to increasing complexity as the stem grows, and (3) managing the trade-off between short-term solution finding and achieving long-term optimality. We compared various algorithms, including reinforcement learning, evolutionary strategies, and gradient descent, to address these challenges. We found that a combination of evolutionary strategies and gradient-based learning of plant models effectively optimizes the target function, often surpassing the performance of reinforcement learning while reducing exploration requirements. We also found that a simple heuristic can balance short-term and long-term optimality. Ultimately, our method demonstrates the capacity for autonomous plant growth optimization, offering a range of practical outcomes. Current data analysis methods are restricted to examining single aspect of these patterns, such as the analysis of a limited student subcohort by a university admissions committee. In contrast, this study applies advanced statistical models, including Bayesian mixture models and multivariate latent profile models, to a comprehensive and representative dataset containing 12 years of enrollment information and 50 academic fields of study. The resulting findings not only shed light on prevailing trends but also reveal novel insights into undergraduate and graduate program pathways. Specifically, these models uncover six primary academic disciplines and three transitional phases, indicating that students often switch between introductory and core courses within their declared major. Furthermore, analysis reveals that some programs serve as natural precursors to others, with physics and computer science naturally leading to engineering, while business and public health are more likely to be chosen later in a student's academic career. Active participation and user engagement are crucial components of social networking, 
fueled in part by user-generated content that comes in various forms such as text, 
images, and videos. While platform algorithms prioritize certain types of content, 
such as images and videos, they often overlook accessibility for users with 
disabilities. In this study, we examined the challenges associated with accessible 
content creation on social media by gathering feedback from 20 participants and 
observing their interactions while using Twitter's web and mobile applications 
to post accessible content. Our results reveal the difficulties users encounter in 
creating accessible content under time constraints, as well as key opportunities for 
improving accessibility on social media by simplifying content authoring and 
raising awareness about its importance. Furthermore, we provided recommendations 
to social media platforms to enhance accessibility and encourage users to share their 
experiences to disseminate knowledge and foster a greater understanding of its 
importance within the social media community. Our research findings can serve as a 
foundation for developing more effective strategies to promote accessibility in the 
future, particularly in areas such as image description, video captioning, and 
emotional expression on social media, and beyond. Ultimately, we aim to inspire 
social media platforms to prioritize accessibility and make it a core aspect of their

We introduce algebraic structures, specifically based on exterior algebras, as valid representations of matroids, and investigate their properties. Specifically, we establish that any exterior algebra structure on a matroid must correspond to either the free or regressive matroid (P-matroid), and show that this correspondence is consistent across various bases of the matroid. This result leads us to the concept of monogenic matroids, which are defined by a free and a regressive matroid structure, and characteristics we identify for such monogenic matroids include them being base-dependent, uniform or rank-1 matroids, and satisfy specific equality conditions. Additionally, we derive a duality result for these matroids, and prove that any monogenic matroid structure on a matroid $M$ implies the existence of a dual $M^*$ with a similar structure. Furthermore, we establish a categorization of exterior algebra structures on matroids as either free, regressive or monogenic, and show that these structures correspond to specific oriented graph configurations, such as bipartite graphs with specific properties, particularly for non-monogenic matroids. We also identify conditions under which a bipartite graph leads to a monogenic matroid structure, and prove the existence of such monogenic structures on non-base dependent matroids such as bipartite graphs with degree sequences satisfying the Havel-Hadamard condition. Finally, we derive a correspondence between monogenic structures on a matroid $M$ and bipartite coverings of its oriented graph, and relate this result to the concept of bimatroids. Additionally, we introduce the concept of exterior algebra structures on oriented graphs, and prove the existence of such structures on graphs with specific properties, such as those satisfying the Turan condition. We also relate the properties of these structures to oriented set-partition problems and prove the existence of such structures on sets with specific properties, such as those related to the concept of Menger products. This work contributes to the ongoing discussion on valid algebraic structures in matroid theory and related areas. It also establishes a connection to the fields of extremal combinatorics and graph theory. The approach taken in this text towards discovering and understanding the properties of exterior algebra structures in matroids is significant, as it leads to new results and generalizations of known outcomes. It also highlights areas of uncertainty and opens avenues for further research in the field. This research delves into the impact of speech recognition errors on the dialogue state tracking task and investigates how such errors can be modeled. Initial studies indicated that errors within the slot values rather than domain or sub-domains led to on incorrect dialogue state tracking. A novel approach to mitigate errors is presented, which involves using Confusion Networks derived from Word Confusion Networks to calculate the ambiguity of ASR output. This ambiguity is integrated into the State Tracking Objective, effectively transforming it into a model for ambiguity-aware State Tracking. Initial findings show that incorporating speech recognition ambiguity can significantly reduce tracking errors without a notable increase in model complexity. Furthermore, the research highlights the distributed data generation methods used to produce high Confusion Network accuracy, which could also be applied to other natural language processing tasks. This work is planned to be extended to the entire speech recognition pipeline in future studies. A corresponding source code can be found at https://github.com/fralexan/cn-dst. 

Keywords: Dialogue State Tracking, Speech Recognition, Word Confusion Networks, Confusion Networks, Dialogue Systems.

We have computed Joyce's enumerative invariants for semistable coherent sheaves of specific ranks and degrees on complex projective curves, which are a more extensive application of the fundamental class $[\mathcal{F}]$, involving higher obstruction theories. This enumeration coincides with minuscule classes in cohomology when the sheaves are of minimal rank. This invariance drove our method of direct computation through an explicit sum on a tautological bundle. This explicit sum was further broken down into a regular double sum over a tautological bundle and a irregular contribution stemming from the cancellation of divergent series. The regular contribution was then reinterpreted as a tautological integrand on the moduli space of sheaves, enabling an almost straightforward computation. The results were verified through comparison with known results from literature when the sheaves are of minimal rank and with Gabbert's cohomology-based enumerative invariants when the rank is arbitrary. This new method of direct computation may be a useful tool for further investigations, while for higher ranks the results were complemented by comparing the computed invariants with Joyce's version through the Fourier-Mukai transform, ultimately leading to a comparison with G\"ottsche's virtual Riemann-Hilbert integrals. This connection allowed us to compute the irregular contribution as the Euler characteristic of the moduli space of arithmetic links, which may be a useful insight. Finally, the results were also complemented by a regularisation procedure that allows the invariance to apply to non-minimal ranks as well. This regularisation was then used to prove that the invariance can be interpreted as a cohomology class when the rank is arbitrary. This insight may be a useful tool for further investigations. We investigate optimal methods for estimating entanglement in quantum systems composed of two qubits using optical systems. Specifically, we focus on entanglement measures defined by optimal local measurements. Our results reveal that these estimation methods can be classified into three distinct categories. Firstly, for entanglement measures that are highly sensitive to maximally entangled states, we propose a simple protocol involving weak measurements. Secondly, for measures that are less sensitive, we outline a more complex estimation procedure. Lastly, for entanglement measures that are not highly sensitive, we propose an alternative protocol involving strong measurements. A detailed analysis is provided to illustrate the trade-off between precision and cost in each scenario. Finally, we discuss how these results can be applied to measurements involving spin, photon number, and entangled photon correlations. Our study contributes significantly to understanding how to accurately quantify entanglement in quantum systems composed of two qubits. Moreover, it offers practical guidance for implementing entanglement estimations in experimental optical qubit systems. Consequently, we believe our findings will have a substantial impact on the development of practical quantum technologies. A Graph Neural Network (GNN) is an effective neural network architecture that processes graph data. Unlike traditional neural networks, GNNs have the ability to utilize graph structure information in their operations. Research has shown that GNNs offer superior performance in tasks requiring graph data understanding. However, most existing studies on GNNs focus on scenarios involving extensive graph data analysis, such as social network analysis and drug development. There is a lack of studies on applying GNNs in real-time wireless communication systems. This work introduces a GNN-based decentralized inference technique that leverages channel state information to optimize wireless communication system performance. Experimental results confirm the efficacy of this approach. The proposed framework serves as a foundation for future research applications in wireless communication systems. The source code is publicly available on GitHub. 

Key Contributions:

1.  A novel framework based on GNNs for decentralized inference in wireless communication systems is introduced.
2.  The framework's first component is a GNN node design capable of real-time inference, optimized for battery-efficient operations and flexible design to accommodate various wireless channel conditions.
3.  The second component is a GNN aggregator that aggregates inference results from multiple nodes while considering channel conditions.
4.  The third component is a GNN trainer that uses simulated wireless channels to train the GNN model.
5.  The source code is publicly available for reference.

This research aims to bridge the existing gap in wireless communication systems research and graph neural networks. The findings and code will be instrumental in driving further research in this area.

A well-known dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short in situations where subsequent vectors rely on feedback from previous inputs. Under such circumstances, the classic estimator can be compromised by a relatively low number of inferences, essentially making it vulnerable to manipulation. A more resilient estimator was proposed, which, despite increased computational overhead, resists adaptive attacks and approaches the ideal sketch performance. Key components of this revised approach include global averaging of estimates rather than relying on local data, and employing a technique that counteracts adversarial bias. A thorough analysis of estimator robustness is provided, along with a new bound on sketch performance that incorporates adversarial resistance, which is accompanied by a discussion on maintaining sketch privacy in the face of adaptive attacks. In online auctions, revenue maximization is a primary concern for service providers. This issue is typically addressed using welfare maximization approaches, but these often compromise revenue. We investigate a scenario in which a service provider can set the level of effort required for the service and choose how to charge, but must also contend with intermediaries that can manipulate user experience. The provider's goal is to maximize revenue, and we examine the cost of implementing mechanisms that yield the highest possible revenue when intermediaries are present. We show that when intermediaries' impact is determined by their actions in a single variable, which we call "transfer of utility," mechanisms that account for this transfer of utility can yield the highest revenue. This property makes use of only intermediate-strength assumptions about the joint distribution of users and intermediaries. For a fixed payment scheme, we found a mechanism that maximizes revenue when the only consideration is computational complexity. This scheme sets the service price based on the effort required and includes a premium that depends on the effort required. This mechanism demonstrates that when intermediaries are present, welfare maximization approaches can also be effective for revenue maximization in certain scenarios. Finally, we discuss how our findings apply to real-world services like Google Drive and GitHub. To measure this synchronization accurately in two-person dialogues, we developed a dynamic approach that combines convolutional networks and transformer architecture to capture both immediate and long-term conversation contexts. Deep learning models can be effectively pre-trained using large datasets of a particular task, such as image classification, before being applied to other tasks, such as object detection and segmentation. However, a question arises as to whether a more suitable method for pre-training exists, particularly one that is closely related to the task of semantic segmentation. To investigate this, we examined whether training a model to predict depth from a single image could provide benefits for segmentation tasks, taking into account that monocular depth estimation is inherently a more difficult task. We compared traditional supervised learning approaches, such as cross-entropy loss, with alternative methods, such as weighted loss, focal loss, and a two-step training process, to determine their effectiveness in producing models capable of generating segmentation masks with depth information. Our experiments involved training on the KITTI dataset and evaluating the performance of these models on the CamVid and Cityscapes datasets, finding that a two-step training procedure led to significant improvements of 8% and 3% in segmentation accuracy and 10% in segmentation recall. Notably, while depth estimation models are more challenging to train, the benefits of this approach for segmentation tasks are more pronounced than those of image classification models. We also found that a model capable of joint segmentation and depth prediction outperforms one that predicts depth alone, but to a lesser extent. Importantly, our results indicate that a depth-estimating model offers advantages over a classification model for pre-training purposes, providing a valuable alternative for semantic segmentation tasks. The model's behavior is ultimately visualized using numerical solutions to a semi-discrete version of the model, derived from a recent study on a similar Holling-Tanner type model. Evolutionary algorithms have seen significant advancements in recent years through parallel computing, resulting in Parallel Evolutionary Algorithms (PEAs). However, a major limitation of using parallel computing in Evolutionary Algorithms (EAs) arises from the asynchronous nature of evaluations, which can lead to an unfair bias towards faster computers. This bias can be mitigated by ensuring a balanced selection of parent individuals for the next generation. Current multi-objective PEAs often use a distance-based approach to select parents, but this method still falls prey to the evaluation time bias. To address this issue, we introduce an innovative parent selection method based on frequency, where the selection of parents is guided by the diversity of individuals, regardless of evaluation times. This approach ensures that all individuals have a fair and equal chance of being selected as parents, thereby reducing the impact of evaluation time bias. Our proposed method has been experimentally validated and found to outperform the existing distance-based approach in terms of providing better coverage and more unbiased results, especially on the TN3 multi-objective function. Furthermore, the selection method's robustness has been tested under varying evaluation time disparities and its effectiveness demonstrated on a multi-objective optimization problem involving a computational-intensive function. The results show that the frequency-based parent selection method can effectively mitigate the evaluation time bias and provide better overall results for PEAs. Moreover, the methodology can be extended to address bias in other parallel computing frameworks, such as parallel machine learning, where asynchronous evaluation can cause bias and affect performance. The research also opens up avenues for future investigation, including the possibility of combining this selection method with other strategies, such as dynamically adjusting the parallel computing process, as potential areas of exploration. We discovered that the unsupervised method of domain confusion is highly effective and requires minimal additional parameters. Additionally, we found that an effective approach to domain adaptation is to apply multiple techniques simultaneously. We also investigated the impact of different training data sizes and found that adaptation methods can improve performance even when the source and target domains have similar sizes. Notably, we found that adaptation is more difficult when the domain size is significantly larger than the number of classes. We found that our top-performing method, domain confusion, achieves an average accuracy of 60% when the target domain size is smaller than the source domain size, and 50% when the target domain size is larger. Recent advances in deep reinforcement learning have led to widespread success across various applications, yet deep RL methods often struggle with two key limitations: efficiency and transparency. High interaction costs can be mitigated through the use of transfer learning, and improved transparency can be achieved through predictive model alignment in a top-down approach. A novel framework for hierarchical deep RL that incorporates inductive logic programming has been proposed, enabling parent policies to influence child tasks via logic rules and domain-specific background knowledge. This framework enables the extraction of a logic representation learned by ILP from a deep RL dataset, allowing the identification of key factors contributing to task performance. Moreover, our framework enables the specification of new tasks by modifying the logic program, facilitating transfer learning without requiring additional data. Experimental evaluations on well-known benchmark domains have demonstrated the superiority of our model over baseline approaches in transfer settings. Blind Image deblurring attempts to estimate a latent image's sharpness and a blurred image, without any prior knowledge of the imaging process. The formation model for this process is often represented as the product of a latent image and a blur kernel, scaled by noise. Current methods that address noise and blur simultaneously use fixed kernel functions, whereas the efficacy significantly depends on the accuracy of these functions. This paper presents a novel approach, Kernel Mixture, that dynamically chooses optimal kernel functions for each pixel from a predetermined set, using a maximum likelihood estimation technique. The method is evaluated on synthetic and real-world datasets and compared with existing state-of-the-art techniques in noise robustness and overall restoration quality. The results show that Kernel Mixture outperforms these methods by achieving higher restoration quality. The source code is available on GitHub under the repository 'KernelMixture'. The experiments were conducted using the 'blind-image-deblurring' configuration.

Formal verification using Hoare logic effectively enables developers to ensure programs' correctness by proving axiomatic correctness.  Yet, a major hurdle arises when translating specifications into pre- and post-data predicates due to limitations in language comprehension.  This paper presents a significant advancement towards resolving this problem by utilizing natural language specifications and translating them into Hoare logic through logical forms.  Our proposed method employs a semantic parser to generate the logical forms of specifications, which are then expressed in pre-post form to verify programs.  This study marks the first major milestone in our project, Natural Hoare Logic, and we have successfully verified several programs with varying complexities, including programs with loops and programs using pointers.  One such example verifies a program's correctness across different input data using Hoare logic and the Z3 SMT solver.  This work is part of a larger project, Natural Hoare Logic, which aims to develop a formal verification framework for imperative programs using natural language specifications written in English.  Our project can be accessed via http://naturahorelogic.github.io.  Our results and program verifications can be accessed via https://dl.fse.unicen.edu.ar/nhl-release. Nevertheless, the presence of a zero-bias peak resulting from the interference of two quasiparticles provided a definitive signature of the quantum pigeonhole effect. noise to the model after training by imposing constraints on the recovery of
the original matrix on the part of the model responsible for predicting matrix
entries. Our approach utilizes the Huber mechanism, a mechanism design technique
that generates privacy-preserving mechanisms by combining likelihood and noise
generation functions. We also present an algorithm for creating a differentially
private model based on the low-rank matrix completion, and evaluate its noise
impact using both synthetic and real-world data sets. Our experiments reveal

original one, and the model's performance is comparable to non-privacy-protected
models, outperforming existing differentially private methods. This method

An implementation of this method has been incorporated into the Nova Nova abstract interpreter. Two proposed tests for extracting bubble components from asset prices, namely the Mehra-Prescott test and the Shiller test, are examined closely. It is demonstrated that both tests yield biased statistical inferences when assets follow certain stochastic processes characterized by rational bubble formation and individual exit times that are randomly distributed and dependent on asset values. Building on this insight, a method to correct bias in asset pricing estimation resulting from bubbles is developed, along with an associated procedure for conducting hypothesis tests that is grounded in theoretical results showing almost sure convergence. This new procedure is inspired by the long-term characteristics of bubbles and is applicable to a broad class of stochastic processes, including cases where parameters depend on asset values. Moreover, it is shown that the asymptotic framework can be used for finite samples when exit times are proximately Markovian. This methodology is applied to S&P 500 data from 2000 to 2019, and the findings suggest that rational bubbles cannot be ruled out based on asset price data. However, asset quality is found to deteriorate when the estimated bubble is substantial. When bubbles are present, as indicated by the Mehra-Prescott criterion, we observe reduced efficiency in capital allocation. This inefficiency is attributed to the fact that market prices do not accurately reflect fundamental values. A novel finding reveals that the risk aversion level implied by the Mehra-Prescott model may be higher than the true risk aversion level when the estimated bubble is significant. This occurs because high risk aversion is associated with reduced asset growth, which in turn can result in a larger estimated bubble. In contrast, we observe lower risk aversion when the estimated bubble is small. Developing CS NLP systems is hindered by the scarcity of CS data. This study delves into utilizing data augmentation methods to create diverse data for improving CS NLP. We examined the current state of CS NLP data augmentation methods and their limitations in the Arabic-English code-switched (Ar-En CS) context. A major challenge in the Ar-En CS field is identifying the most suitable substitutions for words, given that word dictionaries may not be readily available. We investigated the effectiveness of three word substitution techniques: (i) random replacement, (ii) word2vec-based, and (iii) Beitelman's method. A novel approach was also proposed to replace CS words in parallel corpora by leveraging Wikipedia's title and summary information. This study's findings reveal that the random replacement of CS tokens yields the highest BLEU scores, even with a relatively low substitution rate of 0.2. Notably, combining the proposed parallel corpus approach with a small amount of synthetic data (0.2% augmentation rate) surpasses performance with no augmentation. This study's contributions are threefold: Firstly, we identified the scarcity of CS data and the limited explored data augmentation methods in the Ar-En CS field. Secondly, we assessed various word substitution techniques for creating synthetic data in the context of the challenging Arabic-English code-switched language. Finally, we proposed an innovative parallel corpus approach that replaces single CS tokens based on the title and summary information found in Wikipedia, which may be applicable to other code-switching languages such as Urdu-English and Malay-English. The proposed method outperforms other substitution techniques, which suggests that it could be a valuable addition to the repertoire of data augmentation strategies. The study's findings and code are expected to benefit the development of CS NLP systems and contribute positively to the community. We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive, cannot be topologically compact when using the compact-open topology's inherited structure. Furthermore, the same subgroup's action on the surface's one-point compactification cannot be continuously compactified. These results disprove a previously speculated connection in the field. The proof relies on finding sufficiently distinct orbit sequences in highly transitive actions on compact spaces. The findings extend to M-surfaces, a class of compact surfaces featuring a distinguished subgroup of M\"{o}bius transformations. Ultimately, the results imply that certain ideals within the group of orientation-preserving homeomorphisms of the square are not topologically precompact. The study also raises a question about the compact-open topology's properties in this group and offers a corresponding challenge. Our previous fMRI study revealed that the human ventral temporal cortex has distinct areas for animate and inanimate objects.  However, the nature of this animacy system remains unclear.  We hypothesized that it is not unique to a particular category and that it is activated by stimuli that are unique to life, such as movement or the presence of eyes.  To test this hypothesis, we created new sets of stimuli that mimicked the characteristics of animate objects without actually being part of a living category.  These stimuli included artificial patterns that imitated movement, images of mechanical eyes on non-biological surfaces, and graded transitions from one shape to another.  When we measured brain activity in response to these stimuli, we found that they activated the animacy area just as the original stimuli did.  This led us to conclude that the animacy area is not specifically tuned to particular categories, but rather to the characteristics of life, such as movement and the presence of eyes.  It is therefore likely that the animacy area is part of a broader neural system concerned with detecting and processing the behaviors and visual appearances associated with living things.  This system may be essential for understanding complex behaviors and for learning about other agents, capabilities that are uniquely important for social and communicative behaviors.  By recognizing that the animacy area is not specifically adapted to particular categories, but rather to the characteristics of life, we may be one step closer to understanding how it processes the behaviors and visual appearances associated with living things. The vector magnetic field of the Sun's surface is a crucial parameter for understanding various solar phenomena. However, it often cannot be directly measured in modern observations. Instead, it's inferred from a single, measurable quantity called the line-of-sight magnetic flux. Due to the indirect nature of the inference, various biases are possible. For the first time, we assess the presence of bias in common methods of inference. Utilizing a 3D magnetohydrodynamic model, we develop a quantitative understanding of the relationship between the observable and the vector magnetic field. We also introduce a metric to evaluate bias in different inversion techniques. Notably, we find that some commonly used methods, such as the Bel-Rodgers formalism, introduce significant azimuthal bias, whereas others like SDO's Data Analysis System do not. We show that this bias affects not just the azimuth angle but also the polarity of the magnetic field, resulting in incorrect predictions. Moreover, we find that the Bel-Rodgers formalism is particularly sensitive to azimuthal bias compared to other inversion techniques. We explore possible reasons for the bias and suggest a new approach for mitigating it, involving the combination of a magnetic flux density distribution with a specified uncertainty. This method, known as the Bel-Rodgers-Sigma inversion, performs better than the Bel-Rodgers formalism and SDO's Data Analysis System, resulting in lower azimuth bias. Our study highlights the need for a more accurate understanding of the relationship between the observable and the vector magnetic field, especially when inferring a quantity that's not directly measurable. We provide a valuable resource for the solar physics community by enabling researchers to evaluate and mitigate bias in different inversion techniques. This work has significant implications for various solar physics research areas, such as flares, coronal mass ejections, and magnetohydrodynamics. Accurate secure boundary analysis is crucial for practical quantum key distribution systems, but the current approach overlooks a crucial aspect – the randomness consistency of seeds used in privacy amplification. We introduce and verify a quantum key distortion efficiency, which serves as a comprehensive criterion for evaluating traditional quantum key distribution protocols. Utilizing this criterion, we establish a straightforward method for analyzing the secure boundaries of QKD systems with non-uniform random seeds. Simulation results demonstrate that, even at a low random seed quality of 80%, the keys generated can still satisfy the Helstern bound, thereby offering a practical solution for real-world QKD systems. Furthermore, our approach enables the calculation of secure boundaries for time-correlated qubits, revealing that non-uniform random seeds can be effectively utilized to enhance the key generation capacity. Ultimately, our analysis indicates that, under appropriate conditions, non-uniform random seeds can offer the same level of security as uniform random seeds, which is an essential feature in quantum information engineering. A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes a human trainer who assesses the quality of generated policies one at a time, providing the agent with a ranking of policies that maximizes its understanding of the desired reward. Although this approach is highly influential, relying on a more informed human trainer who can effectively maximize the agent's understanding remains a significant challenge. To overcome this limitation, we suggest simplifying the reward learning process by focusing on aggregating policy rankings into cluster groups, allowing even less experienced human trainers to achieve faster learning results. Furthermore, we introduce a technique called Visually-Assisted Cluster Ranking (VACR) that leverages human assistance only for the top-ranked policy within each cluster, significantly reducing the need for human input. By combining VACR with a Bayesian posterior search method, we demonstrate its ability to efficiently discover high-quality policies. To validate our approach, we conduct a series of experiments demonstrating that VACR Cluster Ranking (VACR-CR) can achieve comparable performance to Visually-Assisted Maximization (VAM) while requiring substantially fewer human labels, outperforming other state-of-the-art methods by up to 4.4 times in terms of policy quality. Notably, we observe that even simple human corrections on the top-ranked policy within each cluster can lead to a significant enhancement of the agent's understanding of the desired reward. Image search algorithms that retrieve and identify copied images from databases contain numerous components that compete for resources, including a high-capacity index of image data, a cache of frequently accessed items, and complex query processing systems, each having varying priority levels. These components interact with each other via multiple communication pathways, causing a bottleneck that hinders the system's performance. To address this challenge, we propose an unconventional indexing technique that indexes image pixels inversely, placing frequently accessed images closer together, and prioritizing images that require more complex processing. This innovative indexing method enables the system to determine the most relevant images quickly and efficiently, and our experiments demonstrate its superior performance compared to existing image search algorithms. Furthermore, the system's architecture is surprisingly simple, requiring only a few key components, and we have successfully implemented it as a real-world product called Piq, which has become a leading image search tool widely adopted by software developers. Our case study of Piq's adoption has provided valuable insights into the key factors that contributed to its success, and we believe that our work has the potential to inspire similar innovations in the future. The primary challenge of Fine-Grained Named Entity Typing (FG-NERT) lies in categorizing into pre-defined entity types, often exceeding a hundred, which poses significant classification and knowledge acquisition difficulties. In this research, a novel FG-NERT framework, FGNET-RH, is proposed to address these challenges through a hyperbolic semi-supervised learning approach. By leveraging a graph cone structure, FGNET-RH achieves efficient entity and type embedding generation, enabling pre-trained models to refine embeddings in a coupled manner. Our experiments demonstrate that FGNET-RH surpasses state-of-the-art performance by incorporating multi-view training, also yielding improved scalability through a hierarchical approach that reduces memory consumption five-fold and accelerates inference rates ten-fold compared to existing models. Our code and dataset can be accessed at: \url{https://github.com/autumn-gh/fgnet-rh}. Our evaluation results indicate that FGNET-RH outperforms existing state-of-the-art models, achieving new state-of-the-art performance on several benchmark datasets. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treedepth parameter. Our novel method combines parameterized techniques with SPQR tree-decompositions, extending previous tractability findings on series-parallel graphs, single-source graphs, and outerplanar graphs. We've also established the NP-completeness of the problem when restricted to 3-vertex-degree 4 graphs, treewidth 4 graphs, and graphs with treedepth 5, highlighting the potential for promising fixed-parameter algorithms in these contexts. Furthermore, we've demonstrated that the problem is NP-hard on k-vertex degree 5 graphs, suggesting a degree-based lower bound for the planar embedding problem. Our analysis also reveals the first known non-trivial lower bound for planar embedding, namely that the problem is W[1]-hard when parameterized by the clique-width. This finding indicates that the clique-width parameterization might be the best way to approach the problem, although it remains open for verification. Ultimately, our results provide a comprehensive overview of the parameterized complexity landscape for the upward planarity problem in directed graphs. Crowdsourced image datasets are often marred by inconsistencies such as mislabeled images and incorrect classifications. To counter this, a novel method for evaluating classification uncertainty in image datasets contaminated with noise has been developed. This approach not only pinpoints misclassified images with high precision, but also effectively identifies and excludes noisy data points during training. As an added layer of crowd-sourced dataset reliability, the method also enables the quantification of the inherent uncertainty present in clean data points, thus allowing for their distinct classification under traditional supervised learning paradigms. Furthermore, ensemble modeling is used to quantify the uncertainty present in clean data points, while the Shannon entropy measure is employed to distinguish between noisy and clean data points. When put to the test on the CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 benchmark datasets using a convolutional neural network architecture, the method achieved remarkable results, accurately classifying 95% of noisy data points and accurately rejecting 93% of clean data points. This method has significant implications for improving the reliability of crowdsourced image classification tasks. When put to the test on the ImageNet2012 dataset using a state-of-the-art neural network architecture, the method achieved results that accurately rejected 89% of noisy data points and accurately classified 85% of clean data points. This research has the potential to greatly enhance the reliability of large-scale image classification tasks. Nonlocal games represent a group of computational problems whose decidability status remains uncertain. This research delves into the analysis of two specific types of nonlocal games, namely, games utilizing maximally entangled states that are subject to noise, as well as projective measurements. By demonstrating the decidability of these games, the study effectively establishes a lower bound on the complexity of nonlocal games, with implications that extend to quantum computation. In particular, the findings suggest that if nonlocal games become computationally intractable, the polynomial-time hypothesis may hold true, with potential consequences for randomness extraction and cryptography. Furthermore, the study provides a set of essential tools, namely, the creation of correlations via postselection and noise, which can be widely applied across nonlocal games. This research effectively marks a significant milestone in our understanding of nonlocal games, with the boundaries of entangled states under noisy conditions now fully characterized. Moreover, the study provides a comprehensive overview of correlations derived from entangled states under measurement, with implications for quantum information processing. Finally, the study effectively establishes a lower bound on the complexity of nonlocal games, with the findings having substantial implications for randomness extraction and cryptography. After replicating the original work, the authors encountered issues with device compatibility and app version, which hindered their progress. These challenges highlight potential drawbacks of guided search algorithms, which may not always produce reliable results without further optimization. The authors suggest exploring alternative strategies, such as exploring the call stack from bottom to up, to improve guided algorithms' performance. However, the complexity of these trials often results in underpowered statistical analyses. A primary challenge is to select a subset of treatments with the most substantial effects while maintaining false discovery rate (FDR) control, which is crucial for controlling spurious positive results. We introduce a new approach based on an FDR-controlled detection principle that allows for the simultaneous analysis of multiple treatments without prior knowledge of their properties. This method can be seen as an adaptive procedure that automatically adjusts to the level of dependence within the treatments. Our strategy is to initially group treatments into clusters using an hierarchical clustering algorithm, which achieves near-asymptotic FDR control under any level of dependence. We then apply a simple procedure to select the top candidate treatments from each cluster, yielding an FDR-controlled procedure under mild conditions. Software developers who perform maintenance tasks encounter numerous change requests 
submitted by software system users, presenting the need for maintenance task allocation. 
A crucial step in this process involves identifying relevant maintenance procedures based 
on search terms provided by users; however, developers often face difficulties in 
mapping these terms to industry-specific terms used within the system. To address this 
challenge, researchers have developed a technique called QUICKAR, which reformulates 
search queries to enhance the accuracy of concept location, utilizing crowdsourced 
input and machine learning algorithms. By integrating knowledge from various sources, 
such as data repositories and domain-specific jargon, QUICKAR improves its ability 
to model complex relationships between search terms and industry-specific concepts. 
Experimental findings demonstrate the efficacy of QUICKAR's query reformulation 
process, with a significant improvement in concept location accuracy in 77% of cases. 
Moreover, QUICKAR's implementation is publicly accessible at https://github.com/linusmola/QUICKAR. 
A demonstration of QUICKAR's capabilities can be viewed at a corresponding video.

Adaptive synchronization in interactions, or entrainment, is a key aspect of connections between individuals, as the adjustment of speech patterns in response to others' behavior typically increases the likelihood of continued communication. Entrainment can be categorized into two forms: similar tendencies (similar variance) and similar frequencies (similar rate)) and is often evaluated using acoustic features extracted from spoken dialogue. Acoustic characteristics such as speaking pace, voice pitch, and volume are commonly employed in studies on conversational entrainment. This paper presents a novel approach that utilizes deep neural networks to measure the similarity of interaction patterns in spoken dialogue solely based on the acoustic characteristics of the dialogue, eliminating the need for manual feature engineering and selection. Additionally, a novel dataset called the 'Conversational Entrainment Diverse Responses Corpus' has been developed to support the training and validation of conversational entrainment models, featuring conversations with varied responses and extensive speaker information. Extensive experiments have been conducted to assess the performance of the proposed model and compare it to established entrainment metrics and methods, demonstrating its effectiveness and potential to improve the accuracy of entrainment measurements in interactions. Furthermore, the study reveals that the low and mid-level entrainment characteristics are more representative of the connections between interaction partners, particularly those found in the initial conversation stages. These findings suggest that the proposed entrainment model can be used to predict the likelihood of continued communication in conversations by identifying the mid-level entrainment characteristics. Potential applications of the proposed entrainment model include the development of more accurate conversational metrics and the use of entrainment in the analysis of abusive language in conversations. Future research directions are also outlined, focusing on the exploration of the proposed model's generalizability to various domains and languages. Future studies can involve the extension of the proposed entrainment model to other areas, such as its use in the detection of conversational disorders. This can be achieved by collecting a relevant dataset similar to the one developed in this paper, by establishing a correlation between the proposed entrainment features and the characteristics of the disorder. Additionally, the proposed model can be used in the creation of more natural-sounding dialogue systems by adjusting the speech patterns of the system in response to the speech patterns of the interaction partner. This can be achieved by incorporating the proposed entrainment model into the architecture of the dialogue system. By doing so, the system becomes more adaptive and responsive to the behavior of the interaction partner, which is essential in the creation of a conversational agent that is capable of simulating human-like interactions.
